strengths: Clear conceptual framing that connects prompt-tuning/neologism techniques with the skill-composition formalism of Arora & Goyal (2023), yielding a coherent problem statement (P1-P3) and a principled way to evaluate compositional generalization via ID/OOD skill splits.

The preliminary XOR/XNOR experiment across four open-source LLMs is a nice, low-cost piece of evidence motivating the core hypothesis that vocabulary tokens can encode procedural knowledge, and the XOR vs. XNOR frequency contrast is a clever natural control.

The main experiments use a well-controlled synthetic testbed with explicit sample-skill mappings, enabling clean measurement of compositional transfer (P2) and zero-shot multi-skill composition (P3); Skill Neologisms consistently outperform LoRA and Prompt Tuning baselines under matched trainable-parameter budgets.

Thorough ablations (token length, training composition complexity, initialization) provide some mechanistic insight into why skill neologisms generalize better than the baselines (e.g., limited capacity as inductive bias).
Extensive appendix with hyperparameters, dataset construction, and compute details supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: All core skill-neologism experiments (Section 5) use a single very small model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) on a purely synthetic digit-transformation task; there is no evidence that the method scales to modern-size LLMs or to natural-language skills, which substantially limits the significance of the central claims relative to the paper's broad motivating narrative about 'ever-growing range of skills' in modern LLMs.

Only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL) and seven pretrained skills are tested; the skill space is narrow and the operations are simple deterministic digit transforms, so it is unclear whether findings generalize to more complex, less rule-like procedural skills (e.g., reasoning, coding).

Absolute OOD accuracies remain modest (roughly 0.57-0.85 depending on setting), and multi-skill zero-shot composition (Figure 5) degrades substantially with sequence length, so the method is shown to be 'better than baselines' rather than convincingly 'solving' the stated problem.

The practical recipe for constructing skill-centered datasets for real-world skills is only sketched qualitatively (via LLM annotation or curated multi-labels) and is not empirically validated anywhere in the paper; this is a central practical requirement of the method but remains unverified.

No large/frontier LLM is used to validate that learned skill neologisms (as opposed to the pre-existing 'XOR' style tokens) actually work in realistic settings; the gap between the toy experiments and the motivating claims about modern LLMs is not bridged.

Statistical rigor is somewhat limited: it is unclear how many random seeds were used per configuration beyond averaging across held-out skills, and no significance tests are reported for the comparisons between Skill Neologisms and baselines.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and well-motivated formalism (skill neologisms) that operationalizes three concrete desiderata (P1-P3) for skill-based continual learning, building coherently on the Arora & Goyal skill-composition framework.

The motivating experiment in Section 4 (XOR vs. XNOR keyword vs. description across four open-source LLMs) is a nice, low-cost piece of evidence supporting the core hypothesis that vocabulary tokens can encode procedural knowledge, and it is a good narrative bridge to the main method.

The controlled synthetic experiments cleanly isolate ID vs. OOD skill composition and enable rigorous comparison against LoRA and Prompt Tuning under matched training budgets/soft-token counts, showing a consistent ordering (Skill Neologisms > Prompt Tuning > LoRA) on OOD composition (Figure 4, Figure A2).

Zero-shot multi-skill composition (Property 3) is demonstrated against a sensible in-context learning baseline across multiple sequence lengths, and the result (skill neologisms > ICL) is a meaningful qualitative finding.

The ablation studies (token capacity, training composition complexity, initialization) are thoughtful and produce an interesting non-monotonic capacity-generalization trade-off, adding some mechanistic insight beyond the headline results.

The appendix is unusually thorough (full hyperparameters, dataset construction, per-skill breakdowns), aiding reproducibility, and the limitations section is candid about scope, computational cost, and dataset-construction challenges.
weaknesses: All core method experiments (Section 5) use a single, very small base model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) fine-tuned via LoRA on a synthetic digit-sequence task with a handful of explicitly-labeled operations; it is unclear whether findings transfer to genuinely pretrained LLM skills, natural-language settings, or larger models, which substantially limits the significance of the claims relative to the broad framing of the paper ("towards skill-based continual learning").

The skill inventory is very small (7 pretrained skills, 2 new skills), and the insertion function in the main experiments is a trivial token swap; this is a much simpler setting than the implicit, entangled skills the introduction motivates the work with, so the proof-of-concept nature is not just a stated limitation but a real constraint on how much can be concluded.

Many reported results have large variance across held-out skills (e.g., Table 5: INV-POL kmax=1 C2 = .36±.44; Table A2: INV-POL random init C2(SUB)=.00 while others are ~.8-.9), suggesting the averaged headline numbers can mask highly unstable, skill-dependent behavior that is not sufficiently discussed or explained.

There is no full fine-tuning baseline in the compositional transfer experiments to contextualize how much OOD generalization gap remains between skill neologisms and an upper-bound method, despite fine-tuning being prominently discussed as a comparator in the introduction and Table 1.

Table 1's claim that prefix-based methods can achieve P2 ("*Achievable with skill-centered training") is only partially supported by the paper's own results — Prompt Tuning trained with the same skill-centered data still substantially underperforms Skill Neologisms on OOD composition (Figure 4), so the asterisked claim reads as more optimistic than the evidence shown.

The skill-token-length ablation (Figure 6), which produces one of the more novel mechanistic claims (capacity as inductive bias), is run with only a single fixed held-out skill (ADD) rather than averaged across the six held-out skills used elsewhere, weakening confidence in the generality of the capacity/generalization trade-off.

The construction of skill-centered datasets — acknowledged as a key requirement — is only sketched at a high level (e.g., relying on LLM metacognition or curated multi-labels) without any experiment demonstrating this works in a less synthetic setting, leaving the practical scalability of the approach largely untested.
